unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6: Natural Wonders and Conservation! In this unit, you will explore the extraordinary landscapes of East Africa and beyond, discovering how mountains, valleys, rivers, and wildlife shape the world around us. You will read an original adventure story called "The Citadel of Wind and Stone," set in the dramatic highlands of the Horn of Africa, where a group of young people must work together, make difficult decisions, and learn the meaning of true leadership. Through this story, you will encounter powerful vocabulary, practise important grammar structures, and develop your speaking and writing skills.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: The Roof of Africa: Wonders Worth Keeping
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
High in northern Ethiopia, the Simien Mountains rise like a fortress of rock above the surrounding plains. Travellers often call this landscape the roof of Africa, because its ridges stand higher than almost any other place on the continent. Ras Dejen, the highest peak in Ethiopia, climbs to more than four thousand five hundred metres, and the escarpments below it drop away so steeply that clouds drift past beneath your feet. Wind and water carved these towers over millions of years, cutting deep gorges where small eddies of mist spin and curl against the cliffs. It is easy to see why many visitors describe the range as a natural citadel, a stronghold built by time rather than by human hands.
The mountains are far more than scenery. They are home to creatures found nowhere else on Earth. Gelada monkeys graze on the high meadows in troops several hundred strong, retreating at dusk to sleep on narrow cliff ledges where predators cannot follow. The Walia ibex, a wild goat with sweeping curved horns, picks its way calmly along slopes that would defeat the most proficient human climber. Rarest of all is the Ethiopian wolf, a slender, rust-coloured hunter; fewer than five hundred survive, which makes every single animal crucial to the future of its species.
Because the range is so precious, it was declared a World Heritage Site in 1978, one of the first places anywhere to receive that honour. The title brings responsibility as well as pride. Park authorities employ local people as rangers, guides and scouts, so that the community that has farmed these highlands for centuries makes headway alongside the wildlife instead of losing ground to it. Rangers patrol the trails, repair eroded paths and deter visitors from lighting fires or leaving waste. When erosion becomes conspicuous along a busy route, that section is closed and allowed to recover, and walkers are asked to desist from using it until the grass returns.
The threats, however, are real. The high meadows sit beside villages that need firewood, grazing land and space to grow barley. If too many animals graze one slope, the thin soil washes away in a single rainy season. If companies exploit the range for minerals or uncontrolled tourism, damage done in ten years will take a thousand years to repair. Conservationists deplore such short-term thinking, yet they also understand it: a family must eat today, whatever happens to the mountain tomorrow. The most astute conservation projects therefore link protection to livelihood. Tree nurseries will be planted around several villages next year, and the seedlings will be tended by local school groups. Trekking fees will be shared with the communities whose fields border the park, so a healthy mountain will mean a steadier income than a damaged one ever could.
Why does any of this matter to a student living far from Ethiopia? Because the Simien Mountains are one chapter in a much larger story. East Africa holds some of the most remarkable natural wonders on the planet: the Great Rift Valley, which is longer than any other valley on Earth; Lake Tanganyika, deeper than any lake in Africa; the snows of Kilimanjaro, the tallest free-standing mountain in the world. Each wonder is gruelling to reach, magnificent to see and surprisingly easy to harm. Protecting them is not the work of governments alone. It begins whenever an ardent young reader learns what stands to be lost, asks hard questions and refuses to give in to the idea that nothing can be done.

readings.title: Should the High Trails Close? Two Voices from the Reserve
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every year, when the long rains arrive, the same argument returns: should the highest trekking trails in the highland reserve be closed until the ground hardens again? Last month a student magazine put the question to two people who know these mountains well. Warden Amara has managed the reserve's ranger team for eleven years. Milo is a trekking guide who has led visitors along the high ridge for almost as long. Their answers, printed side by side, show how two reasonable people can read the same facts differently.
Warden Amara builds her case on erosion. "Walk the ridge in August," she says, "and the damage is conspicuous. Every boot cuts the wet turf, every cut becomes a channel, and every channel becomes a scar that widens with each storm. If five hundred walkers cross a saturated meadow, the meadow loses ten years of growth in a week." She points to the numbers her rangers collect: on paths kept open through previous rainy seasons, repair costs rose faster than visitor income. "People think closure is a punishment," she adds. "It is a respite. The mountain needs one, exactly as a runner needs rest after a gruelling race." Amara also worries about safety. Two years ago a visitor ignored the warning boards, slipped near the waterfall and had to be carried down by four rangers. "A closed sign," she says, "is cheaper than a rescue."
Milo does not deny the damage, but he argues that closure is a blunt tool that punishes the wrong people. "Few of the walkers I guide ever leave the marked path," he says. "It is the careless minority who cause the harm. If the authority closes every high trail, it will also close every job that depends on them: the guides, the cooks, the muleteers, the families who rent out rooms in the village." He claims that a full closure would simply push furtive walkers onto unmarked routes, where nobody could watch them and no fee would ever be collected. His alternative is managed access: smaller groups, trained guides and a strict daily limit. "Set the limit low and enforce it," he says. "Confiscate the permit of any guide who breaks the rules. That deters bad behaviour without destroying good livelihoods."
Interestingly, the two agree on more than they admit. Both accept that the meadows are fragile. Both want the fee money to reach local families. Both told the magazine that the final decision should be made by the people who actually live below the ridge, not by officials in a distant office. Where they part company is trust: Amara trusts the mountain to recover if people withdraw, while Milo trusts people to behave if the rules are clear and fair.
The reserve's board will announce its decision before the next rains, and a trial has already been agreed for one valley. The eastern trail will be closed completely, the western trail will be kept open under Milo's managed-access rules, and the results will be compared after two seasons. Rangers will measure the depth of the paths, count the nesting birds and record every rescue. If the closed trail recovers no faster than the managed one, the warden has promised to reconsider her position. If it recovers dramatically, Milo says he will accept longer closures without complaint.
A careful reader should notice what each speaker emphasises, what each leaves out, and how each uses evidence. Neither voice is neutral, yet both are honest. Deciding between them, or finding the astute middle ground, is exactly the kind of judgement this unit asks you to practise.

readings.title: The Citadel of Wind and Stone, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The mountain trail twisted like a coiled rope through the Simien Highlands, dust rising in swirls around the students' boots. Their destination lay far above them: a stone fortress that locals called the Citadel of Wind and Stone. It had once protected an ancient kingdom, and now it served as the final challenge in a national youth leadership programme.
Zara adjusted the straps on her pack and glanced behind. The trail team was still together, though some were slowing. The air thinned as they climbed, and the path grew rougher. Reaching the citadel was no small task. The ascent was gruelling, designed to test not just physical endurance but judgement.
"We need a rest soon," said Rohan, panting. "The sun is hitting harder now."
"If we stop too often," Zara replied, "we will not make it by nightfall."
Tariq, who had taken the lead early, scoffed. "Some of you are too soft. I could do this in half the time."
His tone was always brusque, bordering on arrogant. He had already clashed with others several times, but he was undeniably proficient: fast, clever and athletic. Yet Zara watched him with caution. His actions were often too bold, too fast, too audacious.
Still, the group moved on, following a gnarled ridge where the wind began to howl. Eddies of dust and air spun off the edges, making the cliffs feel alive.
They reached a small respite beneath a rock outcrop by midday. The group huddled in the shade, eating dried dates and roasted chickpeas while the heat shimmered on the stones below.
"This whole hike feels like a punishment," muttered Sana, one of the younger students. "What if someone gets hurt?"
"If they do," Tariq said, "they should not have come. No one forced them."
Zara frowned. "We are a team. If one fails, we all fail. You were told that."
Tariq stood abruptly. "Then you had better keep up."
As he strode ahead, others murmured.
"He will get us into trouble," Kian said. "The guides warned us. If we split, we are responsible for what happens."
"If he antagonises a guide," another student added, "they might confiscate our radios."
"We cannot afford that," Zara said. "Let us catch up, but carefully."
An hour later, they reached a sharp bend where the path narrowed along a steep drop. Tariq stood at the edge, arms crossed, studying the shadowed cleft below.
"What are you doing?" Zara called.
"There is a shortcut through that ravine. Less distance."
"That was not on the map," she warned.
"It will get us there faster."
"It is dangerous."
He stepped forward. "I am going."
"If you do," she said firmly, "you will break the rules. That is a transgression we agreed to avoid."
Tariq hesitated. Behind his eyes something wavered; then pride surged in his chest. "I will meet you there."
Before anyone could stop him, he leapt down the slope and disappeared into the ravine's shadow.
Sana quavered, her voice shaking. "What if he falls?"
"If he does," Zara said, her voice steady, "we go after him. But not now. He made a choice."
They took the long route, slower but safer. Nobody spoke much. Every student was thinking the same thing, and nobody wanted to say it aloud: somewhere below them, one of their own team was climbing alone.

readings.title: The Citadel of Wind and Stone, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
By late afternoon, the citadel came into view. It stood high atop a ridge, stone walls wrapped around jagged rock like a crown. The final climb was steep and exposed. Wind pushed against the students, deterring even the strongest from rushing.
"Almost there," Rohan gasped.
The path forked. One route curved around a sheer cliff: longer, but protected. The other crossed a narrow bridge of rock, fast but perilous.
Zara halted. "Two options."
"The short one looks... outlandish," Kian said.
"Tariq would take it," someone muttered.
Zara did not respond. She studied the terrain, noting conspicuous signs of erosion near the narrow bridge. Stones were loose. A crack split the path near the end.
"We take the long path," she decided.
"No argument here," said Rohan.
They moved cautiously. Wind tore at them, but the trail held. They reached the citadel gates as the sun dipped behind the mountains. An instructor greeted them.
"You made it, and intact," he said. "Any sign of Tariq?"
"No," Zara replied.
The instructor's face grew dark. "He was warned not to break formation."
"He took a shortcut through the ravine. He said he would meet us here."
The instructor radioed the outposts. No one had seen him. Concern flickered across every face in the courtyard.
Night fell. The stone walls echoed with silence. Zara could not sleep. Her mind spun with questions. What if Tariq was hurt? What if they had let him go too easily?
Just before dawn, a call came through: "Found him. Minor injury. He is being escorted back."
Relief flooded the group.
By sunrise, Tariq limped into the courtyard, clothes torn and covered in dust.
"I tripped near a crevice," he admitted. "It took hours to climb out."
"You are lucky," the instructor said. "A few more steps, and the path would have crumbled."
"I was trying to show I could lead," Tariq murmured. "But I failed."
"You were reckless," Zara said, not unkindly. "Leadership is not proving you are the fastest. It is knowing when to wait."
He looked at her, shame in his eyes.
That afternoon, the group was debriefed. Each student had to present a reflection.
Sana stood first. "I learned that fear can be wise. That sometimes the most crucial choice is to wait."
Rohan followed. "I thought I was strong until I realised that strength comes from others."
Zara stepped forward. "I have always been cautious. But I learned to trust instinct and facts together. I did not want to command. I wanted us all to arrive."
Then Tariq stood, and the courtyard went quiet.
"I was wrong. I mistook daring for wisdom. I thought rules were limits. But now I see that they are tools."
Applause filled the citadel's stone walls.
As they descended the mountain the next day, wind trailing behind them, the group stayed close. No shortcuts. No prideful sprints. They stopped to help each other over the loose stones. They moved like a single thought.
At the base, a village child offered them water. Zara handed over her own bottle in return. The child smiled.
"You look tired," she said.
"Not tired," Zara answered. "Just finished something important."
If Tariq had reached the citadel first, he might have claimed victory, but he would have learned nothing. If Zara had given in to pride, the group might have fractured. But they did not. And that made all the difference.

comprehension.question: According to 'The Roof of Africa', why do gelada monkeys move to the cliff ledges at dusk?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They retreat to narrow cliff ledges to sleep because predators cannot follow them there.
comprehension.explanation: The wildlife paragraph says geladas retreat at dusk to sleep on narrow cliff ledges 'where predators cannot follow', so the ledges keep them safe through the night.

comprehension.question: What happened two years ago when a visitor ignored the warning boards near the waterfall?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The visitor slipped near the waterfall and had to be carried down the mountain by four rangers.
comprehension.explanation: Warden Amara recalls that the visitor slipped near the waterfall and had to be carried down by four rangers, which is why she says a closed sign is cheaper than a rescue.

comprehension.question: What do the students eat during their midday rest beneath the rock outcrop?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They eat dried dates and roasted chickpeas in the shade of the outcrop.
comprehension.explanation: In the midday rest under the rock outcrop, the group huddled in the shade 'eating dried dates and roasted chickpeas' while the heat shimmered on the stones below.

comprehension.question: What news arrives just before dawn, and how does Tariq finally return to the citadel?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A radio call reports that Tariq has been found with a minor injury, and by sunrise he limps into the courtyard with his clothes torn and covered in dust.
comprehension.explanation: Just before dawn a radio call says 'Found him. Minor injury. He is being escorted back', and by sunrise Tariq limps into the courtyard with his clothes torn and covered in dust.

comprehension.question: The writer calls the Simien range 'a natural citadel'. What evidence in the opening paragraph supports that comparison?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The range rises like a fortress of rock, its ridges stand higher than almost any other place on the continent, and wind and water carved its towers, so it resembles a stronghold built by time.
comprehension.explanation: You link the citadel metaphor to the fortress imagery and carved towers of the opening paragraph.

comprehension.question: Milo argues that closing every high trail would punish the wrong people. Which evidence does he give to support this view?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He says few of the walkers he guides ever leave the marked path, that a careless minority causes the harm, and that closure would destroy the jobs of guides, cooks, muleteers and families who rent out rooms.
comprehension.explanation: Milo says few of the walkers he guides ever leave the marked path, that a careless minority causes the harm, and that closing every trail would close every job that depends on it: guides, cooks, muleteers and families who rent out rooms.

comprehension.question: How does part 1 make Tariq seem impressive as well as dangerous? Support your answer with two details.
comprehension.correctAnswer: He is called undeniably proficient, fast, clever and athletic, yet his tone is brusque and his actions are described as too bold, too fast, too audacious, so skill and risk sit side by side.
comprehension.explanation: You weigh the contrasting characterisation details in the paragraph that introduces Tariq.

comprehension.question: When the path forks below the citadel, what evidence persuades Zara to choose the longer route?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She notices conspicuous signs of erosion near the narrow rock bridge: the stones are loose and a crack splits the path near the end.
comprehension.explanation: At the fork, Zara studies the terrain and notices conspicuous signs of erosion near the narrow bridge: the stones are loose and a crack splits the path near the end, so she chooses the longer, protected route.

comprehension.question: The passage says the most astute conservation projects 'link protection to livelihood'. Explain what this means, using the tree nurseries and trekking fees as examples.
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means protecting nature in ways that also support local people: tree nurseries will be planted around the villages and tended by school groups, and trekking fees will be shared with the communities beside the park, so families gain from keeping the mountain healthy.
comprehension.explanation: The conservation paragraph says a family must eat today, so the best projects make a healthy mountain pay: tree nurseries tended by school groups and trekking fees shared with the villages beside the park mean protecting nature also feeds local people.

comprehension.question: Describe the trial the reserve's board has agreed for one valley, and explain how it could settle the disagreement between Amara and Milo.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The eastern trail will be closed completely while the western trail stays open under managed-access rules, and after two seasons rangers will compare path depth, nesting birds and rescues; each speaker has promised to change position if the evidence goes against them.
comprehension.explanation: Requires combining the trial's design with each speaker's promise to reconsider if the evidence goes against them.

comprehension.question: Zara says, 'If one fails, we all fail.' How does the rest of part 1 show that she acts on this belief rather than just stating it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She promises the group will go after Tariq if he falls, she keeps the team together on the safer long route, and she urges them to catch up carefully instead of splitting.
comprehension.explanation: You must connect Zara's stated principle to her later choices within the same passage.

comprehension.question: At the debrief, Tariq says he thought rules were limits but now sees that they are tools. What does he mean, and what event changed his mind?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means rules exist to protect the team and help everyone succeed rather than to hold him back, and he learned this after his shortcut through the ravine left him injured near a crevice and rescued only just before the path crumbled.
comprehension.explanation: Tariq's ravine shortcut left him injured near a crevice, and the instructor tells him a few more steps and the path would have crumbled. He realises the rules were there to protect the team, not to hold him back.

grammar.title: Forming Comparatives with -er and More
grammar.explanation: Comparatives weigh two things against each other: short adjectives add -er, longer adjectives take more in front, and than introduces the second item, as in 'The mountain trail is steeper than the coastal path.'
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A comparative compares exactly two things, and its form depends on the adjective's length.
Rule 1 — one-syllable adjectives add -er: tall becomes taller, fast becomes faster, old becomes older.
Rule 2 — two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change the -y to -i and add -er: happy becomes happier, easy becomes easier, busy becomes busier.
Rule 3 — adjectives of two or more syllables take more in front: beautiful becomes more beautiful, difficult becomes more difficult, interesting becomes more interesting.
Rule 4 — use than to introduce the second item: The mountain trail is steeper than the coastal path.
Story link: Zara is more cautious than Tariq, and the highland air is thinner than the air at sea level.
grammar.commonMistake: Double marking, as in 'more taller' or 'more happier': an adjective takes -er or more, never both. Another slip is dropping than, as in 'The trail is steeper the road', which leaves the comparison unfinished.
grammar.memoryTip: Count the syllables on your fingers: one finger means add -er, a -y ending swaps to -i, and three fingers or more mean reach for the word more.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the correct comparative form: 1) The Simien Mountains are ______ (high) than the hills near the coast. 2) Zara is ______ (careful) than Tariq when making decisions. 3) The highland air is ______ (thin) than the air at sea level. 4) Today's weather is ______ (hot) than yesterday's. 5) Walking is ______ (slow) than running, but it is also ______ (steady). Part B — write three sentences of your own comparing two natural wonders, using one -er comparative, one comparative with more, and than in every sentence.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) higher 2) more careful 3) thinner 4) hotter 5) slower ... steadier.
Part B is open-ended (write your own three sentences comparing two natural wonders). Self-check: confirm your set has at least one -er comparative, at least one more + adjective comparative, and the word than in every sentence. Model example — "The waterfall is louder than the quiet stream. The desert sunset is more colourful than the cloudy morning sky. The canyon is deeper than the valley, and it is more dramatic than the flat plains too."

grammar.title: Forming Superlatives and the Spelling Changes
grammar.explanation: Superlatives show that one member of a group of three or more stands above all the rest: short adjectives add -est, longer ones take most, and the word the always comes first, as in 'Mount Kilimanjaro is the tallest mountain in Africa.'
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Rule 1 — one-syllable adjectives add -est: tall becomes the tallest, fast becomes the fastest.
Rule 2 — two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change the -y to -i and add -est: happy becomes the happiest, easy becomes the easiest.
Rule 3 — adjectives of two or more syllables take most: beautiful becomes the most beautiful, difficult becomes the most difficult.
Spelling rules for -er and -est: a one-syllable adjective ending in one vowel plus one consonant doubles the consonant (big becomes bigger and biggest, hot becomes hotter and hottest); an adjective ending in -e just adds -r or -st (large becomes larger and largest); an adjective ending in -y changes the -y to -i first.
Story link: 'Sometimes the most crucial choice is to wait,' and the wind deterred even the strongest climbers from rushing.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping the before a superlative: say 'the best', never bare 'best'. Stacked forms such as 'most beautifulest' are always wrong, and a group of only two things needs a comparative, not a superlative: 'the safer of the two routes'.
grammar.memoryTip: A superlative sentence wears a crown: the sits in front like the crown, -est or most does the boasting, and the group phrase, such as 'in Africa' or 'of the three', names who was beaten.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete with the correct superlative: 1) This is the ______ (beautiful) sunset I have ever seen. 2) Of all the routes, the long path was the ______ (safe). 3) Of the three lookout towers, this one is the ______ (impressive). 4) Of all the students, Sana was the ______ (young). 5) The citadel is the ______ (old) building in the region. Part B — spelling drill: write the -er and -est forms of big, hot, large, happy and easy, doubling or changing letters where the rules require it.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) most beautiful 2) safest 3) most impressive 4) youngest 5) oldest.
Part B (spelling drill): big -> bigger, biggest; hot -> hotter, hottest; large -> larger, largest; happy -> happier, happiest; easy -> easier, easiest.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparatives: Better, Worse and Beyond
grammar.explanation: A small set of adjectives ignores the regular endings and must be memorised: good becomes better and best, bad becomes worse and worst, far becomes farther or further, little becomes less and least, and much or many becomes more and most.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Learn the irregular ladders by heart:
good — better — best.
bad — worse — worst.
far — farther / further — farthest / furthest.
little — less — least.
much / many — more — most.
Examples: 'Zara's plan was better than Tariq's shortcut idea.' 'The weather today is worse than it was yesterday.' 'This is the best solution for the whole team.' 'That was the worst storm the highlands had seen in years.' 'The second campsite is farther from the citadel than the first.'
grammar.commonMistake: Inventing regular forms for irregular words: 'gooder', 'goodest', 'badder' and 'baddest' do not exist, and 'more good' or 'most good' are just as wrong, because better, best, worse and worst already do that work.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the two ladders, good, better, best and bad, worse, worst, until they climb by themselves; irregular forms live in your ear, not in a rule.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill in the irregular form: 1) My grandmother's cooking is ______ (good) than the school canteen's. 2) This maths problem is ______ (bad) than the last one. 3) Of all the students, Zara is the ______ (good) at leading the team. 4) That test was the ______ (bad) I have ever taken. 5) The village is ______ (far) from the city than I thought. 6) He ate ______ (little) food today than yesterday. Part B — review challenge: write the comparative and superlative forms of beautiful, good, bad, easy and far.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) better 2) worse 3) best 4) worst 5) farther / further 6) less.
Part B: beautiful -> more beautiful, most beautiful; good -> better, best; bad -> worse, worst; easy -> easier, easiest; far -> farther / further, farthest / furthest.

grammar.title: Pronouns, Quantifiers and the Future Passive
grammar.explanation: Pronouns such as anyone, everyone, something and nothing replace nouns, quantifiers such as few, a few, all and some measure amounts, and the future passive, will + be + past participle, moves attention from the doer to the action, as in 'The trail will be cleared by the rangers.'
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Key pronouns and quantifiers:
anyone means any person at all: Anyone can help with the project.
everyone means all the people in a group: Everyone arrived safely.
nothing means not anything: There is nothing in the bag.
something means an unspecified thing: Something moved in the shadows.
few means not many, with a negative feel: Few students attempted the climb.
a few means some, with a positive feel: A few students reached the summit.
all means the whole amount or group: All the hikers returned safely.
some means an unspecified amount: Some of the trail was damaged.
The future passive is subject + will + be + past participle, adding by + agent only when the doer matters: 'New trees will be planted along the river.' 'The results will be announced tomorrow.' 'A presentation will be given by a local expert.' Use it when the action outweighs the doer, when the doer is unknown, or in formal notices such as 'Prizes will be awarded at the ceremony.'
grammar.commonMistake: Mixing up few and a few: 'few friends' sounds lonely while 'a few friends' sounds cheerful. Double negatives such as 'I do not have nothing' need anything instead, and in the passive the classic slip is dropping be: write 'will be done', never 'will done'.
grammar.memoryTip: Hear the tone: bare few frowns, a few smiles. For the passive, tap the three-beat rhythm will, be, done before you write the sentence.
grammar.practice:
Part A — choose anyone, nothing, few, a few, all or everyone: 1) ______ can answer this question if they think carefully. 2) I have ______ to do today because I finished everything yesterday. 3) ______ of the players scored a goal, only two out of fifteen. 4) ______ the biscuits are gone! Someone ate the last one. 5) ______ enjoyed the trip; not a single person complained. 6) ______ students volunteered to stay late and help clean up. Part B — rewrite in the future passive so the object becomes the subject: 1) The volunteers will clean the park. 2) The school will organise a conservation day. 3) The chef will prepare the food. 4) The students will write the reports. 5) The city will build a new library.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) Anyone 2) nothing 3) Few 4) All 5) Everyone 6) A few.
Self-check for 3 and 6: "Few of the players scored" carries the negative, disappointed tone the sentence describes (only two out of fifteen), while "A few students volunteered" carries the positive tone of people stepping up to help — use the surrounding tone of each sentence to choose between few and a few.
Part B (future passive): 1) The park will be cleaned by the volunteers. 2) A conservation day will be organised by the school. 3) The food will be prepared by the chef. 4) The reports will be written by the students. 5) A new library will be built by the city.

grammar.title: Comparing Actions with Comparative Adverbs
grammar.explanation: Comparative adverbs compare how actions are done: one-syllable adverbs add -er, adverbs ending in -ly take more or less in front, and the irregulars well, badly and far become better, worse and farther or further.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Rule 1 — one-syllable adverbs add -er: fast becomes faster, hard becomes harder.
Rule 2 — adverbs of two or more syllables, usually ending in -ly, take more or less: more quickly, more carefully, less quietly.
Rule 3 — irregular adverbs change completely: well becomes better, badly becomes worse, far becomes farther or further.
Examples: 'Zara climbed more carefully than Tariq.' 'He completed the trail faster than anyone expected.' 'She spoke less audibly when she realised others were listening.' 'Rohan works harder than most of the other students.' 'Zara speaks English better than she did last year.'
Story link: 'The sun is hitting harder now' compares how hard the sun hits, not what the sun is like.
grammar.commonMistake: Treating an adverb like an adjective, as in 'She runs quicker than me' in formal writing; the -ly adverb needs more, as in 'She runs more quickly.' Watch the irregulars too: 'more well' is never correct, because better already does the job.
grammar.memoryTip: Adjectives compare things; adverbs compare doings. If the word answers how, park more or less in front of it, unless it is a one-syllable sprinter like fast or hard.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the comparative adverb: 1) She can run ______ (quick) than her friend. 2) He speaks ______ (quiet) when he is thinking. 3) They completed the project ______ (efficient) than expected. 4) Tariq moved ______ (reckless) than the rest of the group. 5) The team worked ______ (hard) on the second day than on the first. Part B — write two sentences comparing how two people you know do the same activity, using one adverb with more and one irregular form such as better.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) more quickly 2) more quietly 3) more efficiently 4) more recklessly 5) harder.
Note on 1: quick is an adjective; its adverb is quickly, and this item's common-mistake note explains that formal writing needs "more quickly" rather than "quicker" — this question is testing exactly that trap.
Part B is open-ended (write two sentences comparing how two people you know do the same activity). Self-check: one sentence should use more + an -ly adverb, and the other should use an irregular form such as better, worse, farther or further. Model example — "Sana explains the maths more clearly than Kian does. Rohan plays football better than his older brother."

grammar.title: Reported Speech, Conditionals and Phrasal Verbs
grammar.explanation: This workshop gathers the unit's remaining tools: reported speech shifts tense and pronouns to retell what was said, zero and first conditionals link conditions to results, and four phrasal verbs, get through, back down from, stand up to and give in to, carry meanings their separate parts do not.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Reported speech — shift the tense one step back, change the pronouns, and add that if you wish: present simple becomes past simple, present continuous becomes past continuous, will becomes would, can becomes could, must becomes had to, and past simple becomes past perfect. Requests use asked + person + to + verb, and commands use told + person + (not) to + verb: 'Please close the door' becomes 'He asked me to close the door', and 'Do not take the shortcut' becomes 'The instructor told Tariq not to take the shortcut.' Story link: 'I will meet you there' becomes 'Tariq said he would meet them there.'
Zero conditional — If + present simple, present simple, for things that are always true: 'If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.' 'If one fails, we all fail.' When can replace if because the result always happens.
First conditional — If + present simple, will + base verb, for real future possibilities: 'If we stop too often, we will not make it by nightfall.' 'If Tariq apologises, the instructor will forgive him.' Might, may or can may soften will.
Phrasal verbs — get through means to complete or survive something difficult; back down from means to withdraw from a position; stand up to means to resist someone bravely; give in to means to surrender to pressure. Keep each verb and its particle together: 'I need to get through this problem', never 'I need to get this problem through.'
grammar.commonMistake: Three traps: putting will inside the if-clause ('If it will rain' must become 'If it rains, I will stay'), forgetting the tense shift in reported speech ('He said he is going' should be 'He said he was going'), and splitting an inseparable phrasal verb ('get this problem through' must stay 'get through this problem').
grammar.memoryTip: Report it one step back in time, keep will out of the if-clause, and treat a phrasal verb like a locked pair: the verb and its particle travel together or not at all.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite in reported speech: 1) 'I love reading adventure stories,' Sana said. 2) 'We will finish the hike tomorrow,' Rohan said. 3) 'You must not leave the trail,' the instructor warned. 4) 'Can you help me carry this?' Kian asked Zara. 5) 'I have never climbed a mountain this high,' Tariq said. 6) 'The guides will meet us at the citadel,' the instructor announced. Part B — complete the conditionals and label each one Zero or First: 1) If you ______ (plant) trees, the soil ______ (hold) better. 2) If she ______ (study) hard, she ______ (pass) the exam. 3) If it ______ (snow), we ______ (build) a snowman. 4) If you ______ (add) salt to water, the boiling point ______ (rise). 5) If the group ______ (stay) together, they ______ (arrive) safely. 6) If you ______ (touch) a hot pan, it ______ (burn) you. Part C — choose get through, back down from, stand up to or give in to: 1) Zara decided to ______ Tariq's reckless plan. 2) Do not ______ pressure from people who want you to take shortcuts. 3) If we work as a team, we can ______ any obstacle. 4) Tariq refused to ______ his position, even when he was clearly wrong. 5) It takes courage to ______ someone who is being unfair. 6) After hours of argument, he finally ______ the group's decision.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A (reported speech): 1) Sana said (that) she loved reading adventure stories. 2) Rohan said (that) they would finish the hike the next day. 3) The instructor warned them not to leave the trail. 4) Kian asked Zara if/whether she could help him carry that. 5) Tariq said (that) he had never climbed a mountain that high. 6) The instructor announced (that) the guides would meet them at the citadel.
Part B (conditionals): 1) If you plant trees, the soil holds better. — Zero. 2) If she studies hard, she will pass the exam. — First. 3) If it snows, we will build a snowman. — First. 4) If you add salt to water, the boiling point rises. — Zero. 5) If the group stays together, they will arrive safely. — First. 6) If you touch a hot pan, it burns you. — Zero.
Part C (phrasal verbs): 1) stand up to 2) give in to 3) get through 4) back down from 5) stand up to 6) gave in to.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Comparing Natural Wonders
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose two natural wonders that you know about (for example, the Simien Mountains and the Great Rift Valley, or the Nile River and the Indian Ocean). Prepare a short speech of one to two minutes in which you compare them using comparatives and superlatives. Try to include at least five comparison sentences. Here are some ideas to get you started:
"The Simien Mountains are higher than the hills near my town."
"The Nile is the longest river in Africa."
"The Indian Ocean is more vast than any lake I have ever seen."
"The weather on the highlands is colder than on the coast."

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Role Play: The Leadership Debate

writing.title: Writing 1: Comparative Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a paragraph of 80 to 120 words comparing two places you know. These could be two cities, two schools, two parks, or two natural features. Use at least five comparative or superlative forms.
After writing your paragraph, underline every comparative and superlative form you used. Check that you have used at least five. Then ask your AI Tutor to review your paragraph and suggest improvements.
writing.modelText: My grandmother's village is smaller than the city where I live, but it is also more peaceful. The air there is cleaner, the nights are quieter, and the people seem calmer. Of all the places I have visited, it is the most beautiful.
writing.expectedLength: One polished comparison paragraph of 80 to 120 words

items: The highlands near my uncle's farm are cooler than the coastal town where I was born, and the air there feels fresher too. Life in the highlands moves more slowly than life by the sea, where the markets are busier and the streets are noisier every morning. The highland nights are the quietest I have ever known, though the coastal sunsets are more spectacular than anything the hills can offer. Of the two places, the highlands are calmer, but the coast is definitely livelier, and I honestly find it harder to choose the better one the older I get.
otherAnswers: My old primary school was stricter than my secondary school, though the secondary school is far bigger and busier every single day.
The busy capital city feels louder and more crowded than the quiet fishing village where my grandparents live.
Our new house is smaller than our old one, but it is definitely warmer and much closer to school.

writing.title: Writing 2: Conditional Sentences
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write eight conditional sentences: four using the zero conditional and four using the first conditional. Your sentences should relate to the themes of nature, conservation, or leadership.

7. If our team communicates clearly on the climb, we will reach the summit safely.

writing.title: Writing 4: Short Essay: Conservation Matters
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short essay of 150 to 200 words on the following topic:
"Why is it important to conserve natural environments, and what can young people do to help?"
Your essay should have three paragraphs:
Introduction: State your main argument. Why does conservation matter?
Body: Give at least two specific reasons or examples. Use comparatives, conditionals, and vocabulary from this unit.
Conclusion: Summarise your argument and suggest one action young people can take.
Use at least five vocabulary words from this unit in your essay. After writing, read your essay aloud to check that it flows well. Then share it with your AI Tutor for feedback.
writing.modelText: Conservation matters because a damaged landscape recovers far more slowly than it is destroyed. If we exploit every forest today, nothing will remain to kindle wonder tomorrow.
writing.expectedLength: Three cohesive paragraphs of 150 to 200 words

items: Conservation matters because a damaged landscape recovers far more slowly than it is destroyed, and once a species disappears, no policy can bring it back. The citadel and the highland trails in this unit remind us that natural wonders are more fragile than they look, and protecting them is a crucial responsibility, not an optional extra.

If we exploit every forest and river today, nothing will remain to kindle wonder in the next generation. Those who confiscate land or wildlife for private gain commit a serious transgression against the whole community. Some leaders resent criticism when conservation slows their plans, but an astute government listens anyway, because gruelling clean-up work later costs more than prevention ever would.

In conclusion, conservation protects something no generation can rebuild once it is gone, and the effort required now is smaller than the loss we would face later. If more schools taught conservation early, young people would grow into far more responsible citizens than any law alone could create. Young people can start by joining a local clean-up group or reporting illegal logging to the proper authority, because even one ardent volunteer can make a genuine difference.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Natural Wonders and Conservation" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 12-13 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'atrocity'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Use comparative and superlative forms of adjectives correctly, including irregular forms like better, worse, best, and worst.
Form and use comparative adverb structures to compare actions (for example, "She completed the task more quickly than he did").
Understand and use pronouns and quantifiers such as anyone, nothing, few, and all in your writing and speech.
Construct sentences using the future passive voice (for example, "The report will be completed by Friday").
Convert direct speech into reported speech and report requests accurately.
Recognise and use zero conditionals (facts and general truths) and first conditionals (real future possibilities).
Identify and use common phrasal and prepositional verbs such as get through, back down from, stand up to, and give in to.
Read and comprehend the story "The Citadel of Wind and Stone" and discuss its themes of leadership, teamwork, and conservation.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Roof of Africa: Wonders Worth Keeping" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Citadel of Wind and Stone, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Forming Comparatives with -er and More" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: Vocabulary use and comprehension responses
Grammar, speaking and activity performance
Independent writing, presentation or project evidence
